summary: Extends MPLS LSP ping so the echo reply return path can be selected, to verify bidirectional connectivity and make it more robust. This makes LSP ping more flexible as a diagnostic tool.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network operator pings an MPLS path to check it, the answer has to travel back somehow. This document lets the operator say how the answer should come back, which makes the test reliable and lets both directions of a path be checked in one go.

questions: what is the lsp ping reply path tlv
what is reply via specified path
how to test both directions of an mpls lsp
subtitle: Lets an MPLS ping say which path the reply should take back, so both directions can be checked at once.

tldr.problem: An MPLS LSP ping only proves that the forward path works. If the reply does not come back, the path looks broken even when it is fine, and testing both directions of a bidirectional path takes two separate operations.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds a new reply mode, Reply via Specified Path, a Reply Path TLV that names the path the reply should follow, and a Reply TC TLV that asks for a particular traffic class on the way back.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from January 2014, updated by RFC 7737, and it lets one ping verify both directions of an LSP.

today: RFC 7110 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2014. It is updated by RFC 7737 and has not been obsoleted, so the Reply via Specified Path mode and the Reply Path TLV remain part of LSP ping.

sections.title: What This Adds to LSP Ping
sections.content:
The document defines extensions to the data-plane failure-detection protocol for Multiprotocol Label Switching label switched paths known as LSP ping (RFC 4379). They let the sender specify the return path for the echo reply message, which increases the robustness of LSP ping, reduces the opportunity for error and improves the reliability of the reply. A new Reply Mode, called Reply via Specified Path, is added, along with a new Type-Length-Value record called the Reply Path TLV. The procedures defined in the document apply only to ping mode; traceroute mode is out of scope.

Here, a bidirectional LSP includes both the co-routed bidirectional LSP of RFC 3945 and the bidirectional LSP built from a pair of unidirectional LSPs, one for each direction, associated with one another at the ingress and egress points, as described in RFC 5654. The mechanisms work in both IP/MPLS and MPLS Transport Profile scenarios.

The extension works because an LSP ping is carried out by sending an echo request that carries the Forwarding Equivalence Class information of the LSP under test. That information says which MPLS path is being verified, along the same data path as other normal packets of that class. The four reply modes of RFC 4379 tell the egress router how to send the reply back; the new mode tells it to use the path named in the request instead.
sections.plainLanguage: LSP ping sends a test packet down a path and waits for the answer. This document lets you specify how the answer comes back.

sections.title: Two Problems with the Existing Reply Modes
sections.content:
LSPs are increasingly deployed to provide bidirectional services, and with them operators want to test both directions of a bidirectional LSP in a single operation. With the existing mechanisms, operators have to enable LSP detection on each of the two ends independently. That doubles the workload, and it brings a further difficulty: the router the operator has logged on to may not have out-of-band connectivity to the router at the far end of the LSP, so it may not be possible to check the return direction in a single operation at all. Associated bidirectional LSPs have the same issues as co-routed ones.

The second problem is the reliability of the way back. RFC 4379 defines four Reply Modes: do not reply; reply via an IPv4 or IPv6 UDP packet; reply via an IPv4 or IPv6 UDP packet with Router Alert; and reply via an application-level control channel. The third mode may be used when the IP return path is deemed unreliable, but it requires that every intermediate node support the Router Alert option and understand how to forward MPLS echo replies. That is a rigorous requirement in deployed IP and MPLS networks, especially since the return path may run through legacy IP-only routers. In any case, reply modes 2 and 3 cannot guarantee delivery through an IP network that is fundamentally unreliable, and a failure to deliver the response makes a working path look broken.

Letting the ingress router control the path used for the reply enables an operator to add a level of determinism to the test. When a ping with reply mode 2 produces no reply, and failure of the return path is suspected, the operator can run another ping using the new reply mode and specify a different return path that is thought to work.
sections.plainLanguage: Without this, a broken answer path is indistinguishable from a broken forward path, and checking a two-way service takes two separate tests from two separate machines.

sections.title: The Reply Path TLV
sections.content:
The Reply Path TLV is optional in the LSP ping protocol, but if the Reply via Specified Path mode is requested the TLV MUST be included in the echo request, and its absence is treated as a malformed echo request. If the TLV is included in an echo request, a Reply Path TLV MUST also be included in the corresponding echo reply.

The TLV has a type field of two octets with the value 21, and a length field of two octets covering the return code, the flags and the reply path. The Reply Path return code is two octets and is used by the egress router of the forward path to report the result of processing the TLV and selecting a return path. It MUST be set to zero in a TLV carried on an echo request and MUST be ignored on receipt. The Flags field is also two octets and tells the egress how to process the reply path field when selecting a return path. It is a bit vector in which the A bit, for an alternative path, requires the egress to select a non-default path, and the B bit, for bidirectional, requires the return path to follow the reverse direction of the tested bidirectional LSP. The A and B flags MUST NOT both be set, and if they are an echo reply with the return code for a malformed TLV MUST be returned. When the A bit is set there is no need to carry specific sub-TLVs, and any received ones SHOULD be ignored; the same applies to the B bit.

The Reply Path field is of variable length and holds zero or more Target FEC sub-TLVs. In an echo request it carries sub-TLVs describing the path the reply must follow. In an echo reply it carries the FEC stack information of the return path, when the return path is an MPLS path.
sections.plainLanguage: The Reply Path TLV is the new field in the ping message. It carries a result code, two flag bits that pick between a non-default path and the reverse direction, and the sub-fields that identify the path to use.

sections.title: Choosing a Return Path
sections.content:
RFC 4379 already defines several Target FEC sub-TLVs, and the Reply Path TLV can carry any of them, existing or future, to specify the return path. No assignments are made directly for TLV type 21: the sub-TLV space is the same as for the Target FEC Stack TLV, sub-types for type 1 and type 21 MUST be kept the same, and any new sub-type added to type 1 MUST apply to type 21 as well.

Three new Target FEC sub-TLVs are defined here: the IPv4 RSVP Tunnel sub-TLV, the IPv6 RSVP Tunnel sub-TLV and the Static Tunnel sub-TLV. One use of the generic RSVP tunnel sub-TLVs is when LSP ping is used to check the control plane against the data plane, where using a tunnel rather than a particular LSP avoids the impact of an LSP identifier changing when Make-Before-Break is deployed. They can also be used in the Reply Path TLV to specify a more generic tunnel FEC as the return path.

Together the flags and the sub-TLVs give four options: a particular LSP as the return path, using the sub-TLVs defined for the Target FEC Stack TLV; a more generic tunnel FEC, using the IPv4, IPv6 RSVP and Static Tunnel sub-TLVs; the reverse path of the bidirectional LSP, using the B bit; or forcing a non-default return path, using the A bit. The IPv4 and IPv6 RSVP Tunnel sub-TLVs derive from the RSVP FEC TLVs of RFC 4379, with the same semantics except that the LSP-ID field is omitted and a new Flags field is defined. In that Flags field, P requires the return path to be chosen from the LSPs of the specified tunnel and to be the primary LSP, and S requires the secondary one. The two bits MUST NOT both be set, and if neither is set the return path may be any one of the LSPs of the same tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: You can name the exact path, name a whole tunnel, ask for the reverse direction of a two-way path, or simply insist on something other than the usual way back.

sections.title: How the Ping and the Reply Work
sections.content:
When sending an echo request the Reply Mode MUST be set to Reply via Specified Path and a Reply Path TLV MUST be carried, holding one or several reply path sub-TLVs that identify the return path the egress router should use. For a bidirectional LSP, since the ingress and egress routers know the relationship between the forward and backward paths, only the B bit SHOULD be set. If the operator wants the reply to follow a path other than the reverse direction, the A bit SHOULD be set or another FEC sub-TLV SHOULD be carried instead, and the B bit MUST be clear. Where two unidirectional LSPs are treated as a pair without any binding relationship, the echo request MUST carry a FEC sub-TLV belonging to the backward LSP.

On receiving an echo request, the normal ping processing of RFC 4379 applies. If the egress router does not know the new Reply Mode, it sends back an echo reply with the return code for a malformed echo request received and the subcode set to zero. If it does know the mode, it SHOULD find and select the desired return path. When a path matches, the reply carries a Reply Path TLV identifying the return path and the return code says the reply was sent successfully using the specified path. When no path matches, the reply still carries the TLV and the return code reflects what happened: the reply was sent via another LSP, or via a pure IP forwarding path. An unknown sub-TLV is reported with the code for sub-TLVs that were not understood. The FEC validation results of the forward path SHOULD NOT stop the egress router from continuing to test the return path.

When the return path is an MPLS path, the echo reply MUST carry the FEC stack information in a Reply Path TLV. The destination IP address of the echo reply MUST never be used in a forwarding decision. To avoid that possibility, the destination address of a reply transmitted along the specified return path MUST be set to a number in the range 127/8 for IPv4, or 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:127.0.0.0/104 for IPv6, the IP TTL MUST be set to 1, and the TTL in the outermost label MUST be set to 255. When the return path is a pure IP forwarding path, the rules of RFC 4379 apply unchanged. Sending the reply back over the MPLS path means the reply carries a Reply Path TLV identifying the return path, which gives the ingress router enough information about the reverse direction to check the data plane against the control plane. That is what lets a single LSP ping test both directions of a path. In MPLS-TP deployments where IP addressing is unavailable, the non-IP encapsulation of RFC 6426 applies, the reply mode is set to 5, and the return path is as specified in the Reply Path TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply comes back over the path you asked for, and it describes that path on the way, so the operator can confirm that the return direction really works too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 4379 apply. In addition, the extensions defined here may be used for potential proxying attacks. For example, the initiator of an echo request may specify a return path whose destination differs from its own. Normally such attacks do not happen in an MPLS domain where the initiators and receivers belong to the same domain. Even so, to prevent the extension being used for proxying attacks, the return path LSP should have as its destination the same node the forward path comes from. The receiver may drop the echo request when it cannot determine whether the return path LSP has the initiator as its destination, which means the initiator should choose a source address that matches the specified return path LSP, so that the receiver can make the decision.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the tester chooses where the reply goes, it could in principle aim it at someone else. The rule is that the return path must end at the same node the forward path started from.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has assigned the value 21 to the Reply Path TLV and the value 22 to the Reply TC TLV in the TLVs subregistry of the MPLS LSPs Ping Parameters registry. The Reply TC TLV is a new TLV that the originator of an echo request MAY use to request that the reply be sent with the traffic class bits of the return path LSP set to the value in the TLV. Its type field is two octets with the value 22, and its length field is two octets with a fixed value of 4 octets. It is not limited to the new reply mode and may be used in all the other reply modes as well.

Three new sub-TLV types were assigned in the subregistry for TLV types 1, 16 and 21: 26 for the IPv4 RSVP Tunnel sub-TLV, 27 for the IPv6 RSVP Tunnel sub-TLV and 28 for the Static Tunnel sub-TLV. IANA allocated the value 5, Reply via Specified Path, in the Reply Modes subregistry. A new subregistry for Reply Path return codes was created, holding the codes defined in the document: 0x0001 for a malformed Reply Path TLV received, 0x0002 for sub-TLVs that were not understood, 0x0003 for a reply sent successfully using the specified Reply Path, 0x0004 for the specified Reply Path not found with the reply sent via another LSP, and 0x0005 for the specified Reply Path not found with the reply sent via a pure IP forwarding path.
sections.plainLanguage: The new numbers are registered with IANA: a new reply mode, two new record types, three new sub-record types, and a set of result codes for the new mode.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the return code, flags and reply path.

fields.name: Reply Path return code
fields.desc: Set to zero in a request and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: A for alternative path, B for bidirectional. They must not both be set.

fields.name: Reply Path
fields.desc: Variable length. Carries the sub-TLVs describing the return path.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO ASK FOR A RETURN PATH

cells: Carry the sub-TLVs defined for the Target FEC Stack TLV
Use the IPv4 RSVP, IPv6 RSVP or Static Tunnel sub-TLVs
The reverse path of a bidirectional LSP
Set the B bit in the Reply Path TLV
Any path other than the default
Set the A bit in the Reply Path TLV
